questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Only One Eigenvalue
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=1.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a non-scalar $3\times 3$ matrix that has the eigenvalue $\lambda =1$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$ 

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =1:$

- *Case I.* We may have the single $3\times 3$ Jordan block ${J}_{3}(1).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =1$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{3}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{2}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may have a composition of one $2\times 2$ and one $1\times 1$ Jordan block, say ${J}_{2}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =1$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we have in this situation, we find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =1.$

Computing $A-I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, the rank of $A-I$ is $1.$ Using the rank-nullity theorem, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(A-I) & =3-\text{rank}(A-I) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Recall that the nullity of $A-I$ gives the number of eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =1.$ Therefore, there must be two such eigenvectors, say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}.$ 
So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{2}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Three Distinct Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 8 & 6 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-4.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix that has precisely $3$ distinct eigenvalues. 

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
{J}_{1}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-3)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-4)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & -3 \\ 3 & 7 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =4$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =1$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(1)$ corresponding to $\lambda =1.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =4:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(4).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(4).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =4.$

Computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & -3 \\ 3 & 7 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-4I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -1 & 6 \\ -6 & -3 & 6 \\ -6 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-3.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =-2$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =-3$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(-3)$ corresponding to $\lambda =-3.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =-2:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$

Computing $A+2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -1 & 6 \\ -6 & -3 & 6 \\ -6 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -1 & 6 \\ -6 & -1 & 6 \\ -6 & -1 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -1 & 6 \\ -6 & -1 & 6 \\ -6 & -1 & 6\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -6 & -1 & 6\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A+2I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-3)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Only One Eigenvalue
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=1.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a non-scalar $1\times 3$ matrix that has the eigenvalue $\lambda =1$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$ 

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =1:$ 

- *Case I.* We may get the single $3\times 3$ Jordan block ${J}_{3}(1).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =1$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{3}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{2}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of one $2\times 2$ and one $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, say ${J}_{2}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =1$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =1.$

Computing $A-I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1,$ say, ${v}_{1}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{3}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{2}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0
$$

 

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{3}(1)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.
